art-sacroiliaca.summary: The joint between the ear-shaped (auricular) surfaces of the sacrum and the hip bone, held by very strong ligaments. It transfers the weight of the trunk to the lower limbs.
facts: Synovial in front, syndesmosis behind (mixed joint); very little movement
Anterior, interosseous (strongest) and posterior sacroiliac ligaments; accessory ligaments: sacrotuberous, sacrospinous, iliolumbar
Very limited gliding and rotation (nutation–counternutation); loosens under hormonal influence in pregnancy
clinical: Sacroiliitis is an early sign of seronegative spondyloarthropathies such as ankylosing spondylitis.
It is an often overlooked cause of low back and hip pain.
tus: The front of the sacroiliac joint is synovial, the back a syndesmosis.
Sacroiliitis is an early, characteristic finding of ankylosing spondylitis.

symphysis-pubica.summary: The joint where the two pubic bones meet in the midline, joined by a fibrocartilaginous disc (interpubic disc).
facts: Symphysis (secondary cartilaginous joint)
Superior pubic ligament, inferior (arcuate) pubic ligament
Very limited; widens slightly during childbirth
clinical: Separation of the symphysis (diastasis) in pregnancy can make walking painful.
Osteitis pubis causes groin pain in athletes.
tus: In pregnancy the symphysis can widen by a few millimetres under the influence of relaxin.
The upper border of the symphysis is the front boundary of the pelvic inlet; the empty bladder lies behind it.

ligg-pelvis.summary: Strong ligaments between the sacrum and the hip bone that turn the sciatic notches into foramina, and the membrane that closes the obturator foramen.
facts: From the edge of the sacrum and coccyx to the ischial tuberosity
From the edge of the sacrum and coccyx to the ischial spine
Greater sciatic foramen (piriformis, gluteal vessels and nerves, sciatic nerve) and lesser sciatic foramen (obturator internus tendon, pudendal nerve)
Closes the obturator foramen, leaving the obturator canal above
From the L5 transverse process to the iliac crest
clinical: A pudendal nerve block (in labour) is given just beside the ischial spine, around the sacrospinous ligament.
tus: The sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments stop the sacrum tipping forwards (nutation).
The iliolumbar ligament binds the L5 transverse process to the iliac crest and limits forward slip of L5.

art-coxae.summary: The ball-and-socket joint between the head of the femur and the acetabulum of the hip bone. Thanks to its deep socket and strong ligaments it is far more stable than the shoulder.
facts: Synovial ball-and-socket joint (spheroidal; enarthrosis)
Head of femur – lunate surface of the acetabulum; the acetabular labrum and transverse acetabular ligament deepen the socket
Iliofemoral ligament (Y ligament – the strongest ligament in the body, prevents hyperextension), pubofemoral ligament, ischiofemoral ligament, ligament of the head of the femur, zona orbicularis
Flexion (~120°), extension (~20°), abduction, adduction, internal and external rotation
Medial (main) and lateral circumflex femoral arteries, obturator artery (artery of the ligament of the head)
Branches of the femoral, obturator and sciatic nerves – hip pain may be referred to the knee
clinical: Developmental dysplasia of the hip is screened in newborns with the Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres.
Posterior hip dislocation (e.g. knee striking the dashboard) can injure the sciatic nerve; the leg is short, flexed, adducted and internally rotated.
Advanced hip osteoarthritis needs a total hip replacement; hip pain may be felt in the groin and knee.
tus: The hip is most stable in extension, abduction and internal rotation (ligaments taut).
Developmental dysplasia of the hip is screened in newborns with the Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres.

art-genus.summary: The largest and most complex joint in the body. It consists of the joints between the femoral and tibial condyles (tibiofemoral) and between the patella and femur (patellofemoral); its stability depends largely on ligaments and muscles.
facts: Synovial bicondylar (modified hinge) joint
Medial meniscus (C-shaped, attached to the medial collateral ligament) and lateral meniscus (O-shaped, more mobile); anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments; infrapatellar fat pad (Hoffa's fat pad)
Tibial (medial) collateral ligament, fibular (lateral) collateral ligament, patellar ligament, oblique and arcuate popliteal ligaments
Flexion (~140°), extension; limited rotation when the knee is bent; locking in full extension as the femur rotates medially (screw-home mechanism)
Suprapatellar bursa (communicates with the joint cavity), prepatellar, infrapatellar, anserine bursae
sections: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) stops the tibia sliding forwards on the femur, the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) stops it sliding backwards. They are named after their tibial attachments.
clinical: 'Unhappy triad' (O'Donoghue): combined injury of the medial collateral ligament, ACL and medial meniscus from a blow to the outer side of the knee.
In an ACL tear the anterior drawer and Lachman tests are positive.
Meniscal tears cause joint-line tenderness, locking and a positive McMurray test.
A Baker's (popliteal) cyst behind the knee is common.
tus: The knee has three compartments: medial and lateral femorotibial and patellofemoral.
The suprapatellar bursa communicates with the joint cavity; a knee effusion is felt here (patellar tap).

meniscus.summary: Two fibrocartilaginous rings, triangular in section, between the femoral and tibial condyles. They improve the fit of the articular surfaces and spread the load.
facts: C-shaped and wide; attached to the tibial collateral ligament, so less mobile and more often torn
Roughly O-shaped, smaller and more mobile; connected to popliteus
Meniscotibial ligaments, transverse ligament of the knee, meniscofemoral ligaments
Only the outer third (red zone) is vascularised; the inner part heals poorly
clinical: A sudden twist of the bent, weight-bearing knee tears a meniscus; a bucket-handle tear can lock the knee.
tus: The outer third of the menisci is vascularised (red zone) and can be repaired; the inner two thirds are avascular.
Bucket-handle tears cause locking of the joint.

ligg-cruciata.summary: Two strong ligaments that cross each other inside the knee joint (but outside the synovial membrane): the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) and the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL).
facts: From the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia to the inner surface of the lateral femoral condyle; prevents forward slide of the tibia and hyperextension
From the posterior intercondylar area of the tibia to the outer surface of the medial femoral condyle; prevents backward slide of the tibia; the stronger of the two
Middle genicular artery (popliteal artery)
clinical: ACL tears occur in athletes during sudden changes of direction and landings; a 'pop' and rapid swelling (haemarthrosis) are typical.
PCL tears occur in dashboard injuries (bent knee striking the dashboard); the posterior drawer test is positive.
tus: The ACL runs from the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia to the inner surface of the lateral femoral condyle, the PCL from the posterior intercondylar area to the outer surface of the medial condyle.
The cruciate ligaments lie inside the joint capsule but outside the synovial membrane (intracapsular, extrasynovial).

ligg-collateralia-genus.summary: Ligaments supporting the medial and lateral sides of the knee; they prevent the knee opening sideways (valgus/varus).
facts: Medial femoral epicondyle – medial surface of the tibia; broad and flat, attached to the medial meniscus; resists valgus force
Lateral femoral epicondyle – head of the fibula; a round cord, separate from the meniscus; resists varus force
Both are taut in full extension
clinical: Blows to the outer side of the knee strain the medial collateral ligament; it is assessed with the valgus stress test.
tus: The medial collateral ligament is broad and flat and attaches to the medial meniscus; the lateral one is a round cord that does not attach to the meniscus.
The collateral ligaments are taut in extension and lax in flexion.

artt-tibiofibulares.summary: The upper synovial joint between tibia and fibula, the syndesmosis below and the interosseous membrane of the leg between their shafts.
facts: Tibiofibular joint: synovial plane joint (head of fibula – lateral tibial condyle)
Tibiofibular syndesmosis: anterior and posterior tibiofibular ligaments; it stabilises the ankle mortise
Gives attachment to the leg muscles and separates the anterior and posterior compartments
clinical: A high ankle sprain is a tear of the syndesmotic ligaments and takes longer to heal.
tus: The proximal tibiofibular joint is a synovial plane joint, the distal one a syndesmosis.
In a high ankle sprain (syndesmosis injury) the external rotation test is positive.

art-talocruralis.summary: The hinge joint between the mortise formed by the lower ends of the tibia and fibula and the trochlea of the talus.
facts: Synovial hinge joint (ginglymus)
Lower surface of the tibia and medial malleolus, lateral malleolus – trochlea of the talus
Medial collateral (deltoid) ligament: tibionavicular, tibiocalcaneal, anterior and posterior tibiotalar parts – very strong
Anterior talofibular ligament (the most often torn), calcaneofibular ligament, posterior talofibular ligament
Dorsiflexion (~20°) and plantar flexion (~50°); inversion–eversion occur at the subtalar joint
Most stable in dorsiflexion because the trochlea is wider in front; prone to sprains in plantar flexion
clinical: Most ankle sprains occur in plantar flexion + inversion, and the anterior talofibular ligament tears first.
The Ottawa rules decide whether an X-ray is needed after an ankle injury.
Pott's fracture: in an eversion injury, a deltoid ligament tear or medial malleolus fracture combined with a fibular fracture.
tus: The deltoid ligament has four parts (tibionavicular, tibiocalcaneal, anterior and posterior tibiotalar) and limits eversion.
The Ottawa rules determine the need for X-rays after ankle trauma.

artt-pedis.summary: The joints between the tarsal bones (subtalar, talocalcaneonavicular, calcaneocuboid), the tarsometatarsal, metatarsophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, and the ligaments supporting the arches of the foot.
facts: Talus – calcaneus; most inversion and eversion occur here
Talocalcaneonavicular + calcaneocuboid joints
Tarsal bones and metatarsal bases; the base of the 2nd metatarsal is the keystone
Plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament – supports the head of the talus, long plantar ligament, plantar calcaneocuboid ligament, plantar aponeurosis
Medial and lateral longitudinal arches, transverse arch
clinical: Lisfranc injuries can be missed and lead to chronic pain and deformity.
Failure of the spring ligament contributes to flat foot (pes planus).
tus: Chopart (transverse tarsal) joint: talonavicular + calcaneocuboid; Lisfranc joint: the tarsometatarsal joints.
The plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament supports the head of the talus; its failure leads to flat foot.
